I am a licensed Professional Engineer (PE) with more than three decades of experience in mechanical engineering. I believe the correct action would be to end Optional Practical Training (OPT) and STEM OPT. These programs were created by agency regulation rather than specific statutory authorization and have grown into one of the largest uncapped foreign-worker pathways, competing directly with U.S. engineers for entry-level and early-career positions.  If the program continues, a substantial fee structure is essential.
Entry-level and early-career engineering jobs are the foundation of the profession. They provide the progressive, supervised experience required to qualify for the PE exam and to advance. When these roles are filled by OPT participants, U.S. engineers lose both immediate income and the opportunity to build the credentials needed for licensure and higher earnings.
The scale of displacement is clear. Institute for Sound Public Policy analyses show that in the San Francisco metro area, OPT engineers grew 300 percent from 2012 to 2022 while overall engineering employment grew only 25 percent; by 2022 they comprised 17.7 percent of the regional engineering workforce. In Dallas-Fort Worth, OPT engineers roughly doubled while total engineering employment remained essentially flat. Nationally, in 2023 the United States produced approximately 137,000 citizen engineering graduates (bachelor’s and master’s) while STEM OPT alone authorized an estimated 17,000-plus new engineering positions, plus additional authorizations through other channels. These openings represent a large share of the first-rung jobs young U.S. engineers need.
Wage effects are documented. George J. Borjas (NBER Working Paper 12085) found that a 10 percent increase in the supply of doctorates in a field lowers wages of competing graduates by 3 to 4 percent, with larger effects (on the order of 10 percent) in computer science and mechanical engineering. OPT lacks the numerical caps and wage protections of the H-1B program. Employers of F-1 OPT workers are generally exempt from FICA taxes (IRC § 3121(b)(19)), creating roughly a 7.65 percent payroll-tax advantage that does not exist when hiring a U.S. citizen. Center for Immigration Studies reports and the Department of Homeland Security’s own statements in this rulemaking acknowledge that reducing excess low-paid foreign labor can increase opportunities for U.S. workers and limit wage depression.
I therefore support a fee that is high enough to restore selectivity and internalize costs. I recommend employers required to pay a fee of not less than $100,000 for every year of an OPT or STEM OPT authorization, indexed annually to inflation (for example, the Consumer Price Index). A flat per-year charge better reflects the cumulative impact of multi-year stays and avoids under-pricing longer periods of authorized employment that most heavily affect the entry-level pipeline. The fee should be paid before any recommendation is entered in SEVIS and should also be applied to any current OPT or STEM OPT workers extending to years 2 or 3. 
Ending OPT would best protect the early-career opportunities that allow American engineers to become licensed professionals. If the program continues, a $100,000-per-year inflation-indexed fee for all participants (new and current) is the minimum necessary step.

During the program or after graduating, F-1 scholars who utilize Optional Practical Training (OPT) make major contributions to US innovation in many areas from medical breakthroughs to advancements in agriculture and energy that improve quality of life, create jobs and grow the economy. The proposal to increase OPT fees to $70,000 for initial approvals and $30,000 for renewals is unreasonable and harmful to workers. International and domestic workers alike are in need of policies that protect and lift standards for all workers, safeguard their rights in the workplace, and prevent employers from suppressing wages and benefits or pitting workers against each other. I am Tamunonye Cheetham-West, a Gibbs Assistant Professor in the math department at Yale University. I write regarding Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 a proposed rule charging fees of up to $70,000 and $30,000 for OPT fees in the first and in further instances respectively.

I am an F-1 chemistry Ph.D. student at a U.S. research university and expect to graduate in 2027. My research involves mass spectrometry, laser spectroscopy, vacuum instrumentation, and the electronic structure of actinide-containing molecules. OPT would allow me to apply this specialized training in a practical setting directly related to my degree. The proposed fees would create a serious barrier to that educational opportunity.

The proposal does not adequately protect students already pursuing their degrees (Sections V.C and VI).

Doctoral education requires years of sustained work. Students approaching graduation have already invested substantial time and effort in specialized training and are making plans under the existing regulatory framework. A 60-day transition after publication of a final rule cannot reasonably accommodate the disruption caused by a new financial requirement of this magnitude.

I recognize that OPT requires authorization and is not guaranteed. However, the opportunity to apply for an established training program is materially different from an opportunity conditioned on a new $70,000 payment. Applying the fee only to recommendations issued after the effective date would still disrupt students who enrolled years earlier. DHS should preserve access under the existing fee framework for currently enrolled students, including their subsequent STEM OPT extensions.

Requiring schools to pay does not eliminate the burden on students (Sections V.A and VI).

The proposal requires educational institutions to pay before recommending students for OPT. If institutions cannot absorb these costs, they may limit recommendations or pass costs to students or other parties. Either outcome could prevent otherwise eligible students from participating for reasons unrelated to the legitimacy or educational value of their training.

For a graduate student, a $70,000 charge would be an extraordinary financial burden. Nor can I assume that my university or a prospective employer would pay it. Access to legitimate practical training should not depend on a student's personal wealth or an institution's ability to make such a large payment.

A uniform financial barrier is poorly targeted to fraud prevention (Section IV).

I support meaningful oversight, verification of legitimate training, and enforcement against fraudulent schools and employers. However, the ability to pay a large fee does not establish that a training opportunity is genuine, and inability to pay does not establish fraud.

DHS should explain, with evidence, why these specific fee amounts are necessary and how they would distinguish fraudulent participation from compliant participation. It should evaluate less burdensome alternatives, including risk-based audits, verification of employers and training activities, and enforcement focused on documented violations. Any oversight fee should be transparent, proportionate, and supported by the actual cost of administering that oversight.

DHS should give greater weight to the loss of legitimate scientific training opportunities (Section VII.A).

My doctoral work has developed skills in experimental design, instrument troubleshooting, and analysis of complex scientific data. Practical training would help me extend those skills beyond my dissertation research. A financial barrier that prevents participation could also deprive U.S. research teams and employers of relevant expertise. DHS should evaluate these effects rather than treating reduced participation as evidence that program integrity has improved.

For these reasons, I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fees. I also oppose the alternative of charging the $70,000 initial fee again at each higher educational level. If DHS proceeds with changes, it should protect currently enrolled students and adopt targeted, evidence-based oversight measures that preserve access to legitimate OPT and STEM OPT.

Docket ID: ICEB-2026-0100
Subject: Comment in Support of Proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) Fees
I am writing as a U.S. citizen to express my strong support for the Department of Homeland Security’s proposed rule to establish structural fees for the Optional Practical Training (OPT) and STEM OPT programs.
The primary duty of the United States government must be to protect and prioritize its own citizens. Currently, many American citizens and permanent residents are facing extreme difficulty finding employment within their fields, particularly in technology and STEM sectors. No other country’s government implements programs that favor foreign nationals over their own domestic workforce in the way current U.S. policies do. By exempting employers from certain payroll taxes (such as FICA) for F-1 students on OPT, the current system inadvertently gives a financial advantage to foreign graduates over qualified American workers.
Implementing these fees is a necessary step to correct this imbalance and protect the domestic labor market. By adjusting the cost of the program, the rule helps ensure that U.S. workers are not placed at a disadvantage for entry-level positions and specialized roles. Furthermore, placing the regulatory cost on the SEVP-certified institutions that profit from international enrollment ensures that the true administrative burden of the program is properly funded.
I urge DHS to finalize and implement this rule as proposed to fulfill its obligation to protect the domestic workforce and prioritize employment opportunities for American citizens.
Thank you for considering my feedback.

Public Comment on DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100: Proposed OPT Fees

I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and $30,000 for subsequent OPT participation. These extraordinary fees are disproportionate to the stated objectives, insufficiently justified by the available evidence, and likely to impose substantial costs on legitimate students, educational institutions, employers, and the U.S. economy.

1. The evidence of fraud does not justify these specific fees.

DHS cites examples of fraud, shell companies, and questionable employment arrangements. However, evidence that fraud exists does not establish its prevalence across the overall OPT population or demonstrate that imposing enormous fees on all participants is an effective solution.

DHS should provide verified data on the percentage of OPT participants involved in confirmed fraud, distinguish proven violations from suspected cases, quantify the resulting harm, and explain how these specific fees would prevent future violations. Without this evidence, the proposed policy risks penalizing legitimate participants for misconduct they did not commit.

2. The proposed fee amounts lack adequate justification.

Why $70,000 and $30,000? DHS should provide a transparent explanation of how these amounts were calculated and how they relate to actual administrative costs, enforcement expenses, or measurable reductions in fraud.

If the primary purpose is to discourage participation, DHS should acknowledge that the policy may exclude legitimate students and explain why this outcome is necessary and proportionate. A policy should not be considered justified merely because an extraordinarily high price discourages people from participating.

3. The policy is poorly targeted at the actual problem.

The proposed fees apply regardless of whether a student, employer, or educational institution has engaged in misconduct. Legitimate students and compliant institutions could face the same financial barriers as those associated with fraudulent arrangements.

If DHS’s concerns involve shell companies, nonexistent jobs, and false employment records, targeted investigations, employer verification, compliance audits, and stronger penalties for proven violations would address these problems more directly. DHS should demonstrate why a blanket fee is more effective than these alternatives.

4. The economic analysis acknowledges significant uncertainty.

DHS acknowledges uncertainty about how much OPT participation would decline and the difficulty of precisely quantifying the resulting opportunity costs. Nevertheless, the proposed fees could fundamentally change hiring decisions, university recommendations, and students’ employment opportunities.

The analysis should rigorously assess the potential effects on international student enrollment, employer recruitment, small businesses, research, innovation, productivity, and U.S. competitiveness. A decline in OPT participation should not automatically be treated as a policy success if it also means lost employment opportunities, reduced economic activity, and qualified graduates taking their skills elsewhere.

Where substantial uncertainty exists, DHS should provide transparent sensitivity analyses and explain how its conclusions change under different assumptions about participation, employer demand, and cost-sharing arrangements.

5. DHS has not adequately demonstrated why less burdensome alternatives are insufficient.

The agency should compare the effectiveness and costs of the proposed fees against risk-based audits, enhanced employment verification, stronger oversight of institutions with documented compliance problems, and penalties for confirmed fraud.

Administrative convenience is not sufficient justification for imposing extraordinary financial burdens on legitimate participants. DHS must demonstrate that the proposed fees would produce meaningful improvements in program integrity that could not be achieved through more targeted enforcement measures.

6. The proposal could harm U.S. workers and the broader economy rather than benefit them.

DHS identifies protecting U.S. workers as an objective, but reducing OPT participation does not automatically create additional employment opportunities for American workers. Employers might instead reduce hiring, delay projects, abandon research, or move investment and talent elsewhere.

DHS should provide evidence of the specific labor-market harms it seeks to address and demonstrate that the proposed fees would improve employment outcomes for U.S. workers. It should also assess the consequences for universities, local economies, and the country’s ability to attract international talent.

Conclusion

I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fees in their current form.

Fraud prevention and protection of U.S. workers are legitimate objectives, but they do not justify a policy without a convincing evidentiary foundation.

I strongly oppose the proposed rule establishing $70,000 and $30,000 fees for Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendations and respectfully urge DHS to withdraw it.

I recognize the importance of protecting program integrity and preventing fraud. The proposal itself acknowledges that the collected fees would be deposited into the U.S. Treasury rather than directly funding OPT oversight. This raises a fundamental question about the relationship between the proposed financial burden and the stated regulatory objectives.

The economic consequences also deserve much greater consideration. DHS estimates approximately $12.8 billion in annualized transfers and $4.1 billion in annualized economic costs under its primary estimates. These are substantial burdens on universities, students, and the broader economy, with potentially serious consequences for educational opportunities and scientific research.

OPT is an important part of the U.S. higher education and research ecosystem. Restricting access through exceptionally high fees would discourage international talent, weaken universities' ability to attract and retain highly trained graduates, and undermine American scientific competitiveness.

I am particularly concerned that the proposal would impose substantial costs on legitimate participants without adequately distinguishing them from institutions or individuals engaged in fraud. Financial resources should not become a substitute for meaningful compliance assessment.

I also urge DHS to reconsider the proposed transition provisions, under which students already participating in OPT could face a $70,000 fee for a subsequent recommendation if no initial fee had previously been paid.

For these reasons, I respectfully request that DHS withdraw the proposed rule and pursue more proportionate, evidence-based measures to protect OPT program integrity.

Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 — Comment opposing the proposed Optional Practical Training Fees

I am an international graduate student in F-1 status, studying design. I came to the United States to study and I pay full tuition. I strongly oppose this proposed rule and ask DHS to withdraw it.

1. Section IV.C and V.A: the "fee" recovers no cost and is a penalty, not a fee.
DHS states that the money would go to the Treasury as a miscellaneous receipt, that ICE would not use it, and that its purpose is deterrence. A $70,000 charge that pays for no government service is not a fee. The "time and conditions" authority in INA 214(a) has never been read to let DHS raise billions of dollars in revenue. When Congress wants a large immigration charge, such as the H-1B fees under ACWIA or the SEVIS fee under IIRIRA section 641, it writes the amount or the cost basis into a statute. DHS's own analysis estimates transfers of about $12.8 billion per year. A charge of that size needs to come from Congress, not from a rule.

2. Section IV.C: the fee does not target fraud. It targets everyone.
The rule describes "visa mills" and specific bad actors, but the fee falls equally on every student at every school. DHS considered extending STEM OPT safeguards such as the I-983 training plan and site visits, and rejected them mainly because they would cost the government more effort. Choosing the cheapest tool over the one that actually fits the problem is not reasoned decision-making. If certain schools or employers are abusing OPT, DHS already has the power to investigate them and withdraw SEVP certification.

3. Section IV.C: the fee selects for wealth, not for "the most promising students."
DHS admits schools may pass the fee on to students. For a design student, $70,000 is more than a typical first-year salary in my field. Practical training is part of how design is learned: you only understand interaction design by building real products with real teams. Under this rule, an art and design school either pays $70,000 per student, which art schools cannot afford, or OPT disappears for us. The students who could still participate would be the ones with family money, not the most talented ones.

4. Section V.A: charging $70,000 for pre-completion OPT and $30,000 more for post-completion OPT punishes the educational use of the program.
Pre-completion OPT is the clearest case of training that is part of a course of study. Charging $100,000 to the same student for one degree contradicts DHS's stated goal of keeping OPT tied to education. I also oppose the alternative of charging the $70,000 again at each new degree level.

5. Section VI: DHS dismisses the reliance interests of students who are already here.
Footnote 124 acknowledges that current students are in a different position from prospective ones, then gives that difference no weight. Students like me chose our programs, paid tuition, and moved our lives here based on rules that have been in place for decades and that the D.C. Circuit upheld in 2022. Changing the cost of OPT from about $500 to $70,000 in the middle of a degree is exactly the kind of reliance interest the APA requires an agency to take seriously. At a minimum, any final rule should exempt every student who is enrolled in F-1 status on the date the final rule is published.

6. Section I: 30 days is not enough.
This rule has estimated 10-year transfers of over $100 billion and affects more than a million students and thousands of schools. I ask DHS to extend the comment period to at least 60 days.

International students pay full tuition, support U.S. universities, and many of us go on to create jobs here. OPT is a short period of training connected to our degrees. Please withdraw this proposed rule.

Docket ICEB-2026-0100 — Opposition to Proposed OPT Fees

Dear Department of Homeland Security,

I am writing as a concerned parent to strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee, including STEM OPT extensions.

My elder son enrolled at the Georgia Institute of Technology (Georgia Tech) in Fall 2024 to pursue his undergraduate degree in Computer Science. He expects to graduate in Spring 2027.

When he enrolled, our family made significant educational, financial, and career decisions based on the regulations and opportunities available at that time. The possibility of obtaining lawful practical training after graduation was an important part of our planning.

We understood that OPT required government approval. However, we could not have anticipated a $70,000 fee being introduced more than two years after he began college.

Now, just months before graduation, this proposal creates uncertainty about his future. Our family has invested substantial financial resources, and my son has committed years toward completing his degree.

**1. Reliance Interests and Grandfathering — Section VI**

DHS acknowledges that students already enrolled in American universities are differently situated from prospective students. Nevertheless, the proposal would apply new fees to future OPT recommendations, even for students who began their education years earlier.

My son enrolled in Fall 2024, while this proposal was published in October 2026. Applying these fees near graduation does not adequately recognize our existing commitments.

Had these fees been known in 2024, our family would have evaluated our educational decisions differently.

I request that DHS grandfather students enrolled before October 8, 2026, allowing them to pursue eligible initial OPT and STEM OPT extensions under the existing fee framework.

**2. Inadequate Transition Period — Section V.C**

The proposed 60-day transition period is insufficient for students who have already invested years in their education.

Students approaching graduation cannot easily change universities, recover tuition expenses, or reverse career decisions.

A meaningful transition should recognize enrollment dates rather than only future OPT recommendation dates.

**3. Excessive Financial Burden — Sections IV.C and V.A**

The proposed fees could total $100,000 for initial OPT followed by a STEM OPT extension.

Families already invest heavily in tuition, housing, health insurance, and educational expenses.

Although universities would pay these fees, DHS acknowledges that costs could be passed to students, families, or employers.

This could make practical training inaccessible to qualified students because of financial limitations.

**4. Academic Merit and Fair Opportunity**

OPT eligibility should depend on academic qualifications, immigration compliance, and genuine training related to a student's field of study.

A university's ability to pay $70,000 does not determine whether a student is talented, qualified, or compliant.

Financial capacity should not replace academic merit in determining access to practical training.

**5. Targeted Fraud Prevention — Section IV.A**

I support DHS's efforts to prevent immigration fraud and protect American workers.

However, legitimate students should not face extraordinary financial barriers because of misconduct committed by others.

Stronger employer verification, risk-based inspections, institutional oversight, and enforcement against fraudulent organizations would more directly address these concerns.

**6. Impact on American Higher Education**

American universities attract talented students through educational excellence, research, and professional opportunities.

Unexpected OPT fees could affect enrollment decisions, legitimate training opportunities, and the ability of institutions and employers to support graduates.

DHS should carefully evaluate these consequences.

**My Requests**

I request that DHS withdraw or reconsider the proposed fees, grandfather students enrolled before October 8, 2026, protect eligible STEM OPT extensions, reconsider the 60-day transition period, and prioritize targeted fraud prevention.

For our family, this proposal directly affects my son's future. He began college in Fall 2024 hoping to complete his education and gain legitimate practical experience after graduation.

We have invested years of effort and substantial financial resources. Changing these requirements shortly before graduation creates hardship and uncertainty.

I urge DHS to protect students who made educational commitments in good faith under existing regulations.

Thank you for considering my comments.

Sincerely,

A Concerned Parent of a Georgia Tech Student

Docket ID: ICEB-2026-0100
Subject: Strong Support for the Proposed Restructuring of OPT Program Fees
I am writing to express my strong support for the proposed regulatory fees for the Optional Practical Training (OPT) and STEM OPT extensions. As an employee in the technology industry, I believe it is critical to re-evaluate how entry-level tech roles are distributed in our country.
While there is an obvious benefit to importing elite, world-class scientists and researchers who bring unique value to the United States, the same logic does not apply to entry-level roles. Our government should be prioritizing our own citizens—like my child, a straight-A computer science graduate—for entry-level jobs and internships so they can gain experience and build their careers. Instead, under the current system, foreign nationals are given a tax-subsidized advantage over citizens to earn money here, even though they often do not share the same long-term civic or tax obligations as American families.
Furthermore, the lack of strict oversight in the entry-level OPT pipeline introduces severe operational risks for American companies. In my own direct professional experience, the technology company where I work hired a foreign national for an entry-level engineering position, and she ultimately stole all of our proprietary source code, transferring it directly to her personal accounts before leaving. When temporary workers have no lasting ties or commitment to our nation, there is a much higher risk of intellectual property theft that harms American businesses and workers alike.
Imposing a substantial financial fee on SEVP-certified institutions is a necessary measure to naturally regulate the entry-level labor supply, reduce corporate exploitation of cheaper foreign labor, and protect the security of American innovation. I strongly urge DHS to implement this rule immediately.

I fully support the proposed rule, as I believe it could significantly reduce student visa fraud. Over the past few years, the U.S. government has granted around 400,000 F-1 visas annually. This is a massive influx for the system to absorb, especially given the current challenges with inflation, the housing crisis, and the widespread layoffs caused by the rise of artificial intelligence.

Because the majority of international students come from India, the financial strain on them is amplified by purchasing power parity. A dollar has nearly four times more purchasing power in India than in the U.S., which means the reverse is also true: Indian students must effectively expend four times the local economic effort to cover the same expenses as a U.S. citizen. This disparity forces many families to take on devastating debts, often requiring them to put up their homes and properties as collateral.

Consequently, these students face immense pressure and feel they cannot afford to return home empty-handed. Driven by the need to survive and repay their massive debts, most of them ultimately resort to fraudulent methods—whether through legal loopholes or illegal means—just to remain in the country and earn a living.

However, I do think it is unfair for currently enrolled students to be affected by the new rule. This is especially true for those who are already in the U.S. and want to pursue higher education—such as a Ph.D. or another degree in emerging fields like AI—to upskill themselves. Therefore, I believe these rules should definitely come into effect, but only for students who are newly admitted and enrolling from their home countries moving forward—perhaps targeting those whose F-1 visas are stamped in 2027 or later.

There was a time and a place where this program was appropriate. That time is not now. We have raised an entire generation of STEM grads that can no longer find jobs because this program is being abused. I support ending the programs or all restrictions to limit them and protect our college grads from unfair practices that hurt them in getting started in their careers.

To the Department of Homeland Security:

I respectfully oppose the proposed $70,000 initial Optional Practical Training fee and $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT recommendations. I urge DHS to withdraw this fee structure and preserve affordable access to legitimate, degree-related practical training.

As a scientist who works in biotechnology and bioinformatics, I am concerned about the consequences for scientific research, workforce development, and medical innovation. Practical training allows graduates to apply specialized knowledge, develop professional skills, and contribute to research teams. Access to these opportunities should depend on qualifications and compliance with program requirements, rather than the ability to finance an extraordinary fee.

Although educational institutions would be responsible for payment under the proposal, that does not eliminate the financial burden. Institutions may limit recommendations, pass costs to students, or seek payment from employers. Qualified graduates could consequently lose training opportunities even when they meet every other eligibility requirement.

In biotechnology, many valuable training opportunities exist at small companies, academic laboratories, and organizations operating under limited research budgets. A substantial additional fee could make it financially impractical for these organizations to support a graduate’s participation. DHS should evaluate the potential effects on research continuity, federally funded projects, and the development of treatments and diagnostic technologies that could benefit American patients.

I support protecting American workers and addressing fraud. However, the ability to pay is not a reliable measure of whether a training opportunity is legitimate. DHS should explain the evidence supporting these particular fee amounts and assess whether they would deter misconduct or primarily discourage lawful participation. Reduced participation alone should not be treated as proof of successful fraud prevention.

More targeted approaches deserve meaningful consideration, including verification that training relates to the student’s degree, focused compliance reviews, employer accountability, and enforcement of applicable worker protections. These approaches would address specific problems without imposing the same financial barrier on compliant students and institutions.

I also urge DHS to consider the reliance interests of students already enrolled in U.S. educational programs and graduates already participating in OPT. They may have invested years of study and substantial financial resources with the expectation that they could pursue practical training under the existing framework. A short transition period would not adequately account for those commitments.

The agency should also examine whether these fees could increase students’ debt or dependence on employers willing to finance participation. Making workers financially dependent on a limited number of sponsors could undermine their ability to leave unsuitable employment or report mistreatment.

For these reasons, I request that DHS withdraw the proposed fee structure. If the agency pursues an alternative, it should provide a transparent justification, evaluate substantially lower fees and meaningful waivers, and protect students and participants with existing educational commitments.

The United States benefits when its educational institutions can translate advanced training into scientific discovery and productive work. I urge DHS to protect that pathway through proportionate oversight and evidence-based enforcement.

Thank you for considering my comment.

Public Comment: DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees

I respectfully oppose the proposed $70,000 fee for a student's first OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each later recommendation. DHS should withdraw this proposal and use targeted, risk-based measures against documented fraud. Please review my attached full comment, which provides the full analysis and references.

These fees are disproportionate and would deny OPT to many qualified students. Although schools must formally pay, DHS acknowledges that institutions may pass the cost to students, employers, or others. Many public and smaller institutions cannot absorb $70,000 or $100,000 per student. Access would depend less on eligibility and merit than on institutional wealth and financial support. Law-abiding students at less wealthy schools would suffer most.
International students already face status, reporting, unemployment, work-authorization, and degree-related-employment rules. STEM OPT adds E-Verify, Form I-983 training plans, compensation and non-displacement attestations, evaluations, and possible site visits. Fraud should be addressed through audits, analytics, training, site visits, and enforcement against offending schools, employers, or individuals, not via a hefty fee on compliant participants.
Many employers restrict hiring to U.S. citizens or permanent residents or reject applicants who may later need sponsorship. OPT work must directly relate to the graduate's field of study and is temporary. A fee designed to eliminate participants does not distinguish fraud from lawful training or target employers engaged in wage or displacement abuses.

The proposal would harm U.S. science and economic competitiveness. International master's and doctoral students spend years contributing in laboratories and research groups involving energy, defense-related technologies, advanced materials, computing, health, and manufacturing. Ph.D. researchers produce publications, patents, prototypes, data, software, and teaching contributions before seeking post-degree training. OPT lets U.S.-educated graduates apply that knowledge in American laboratories, companies, startups, hospitals, and universities. Driving them away after training transfers knowledge, entrepreneurship, tax revenue, and innovative capacity to competing countries.

The National Science Board reported that foreign-born workers were 43% of doctorate-level scientists and engineers in 2021; temporary visa holders earned substantial shares of advanced degrees in engineering, computer science, and mathematics. Research finds that immigrant inventors contribute disproportionately to U.S. patenting and generate productivity spillovers for U.S.-born collaborators. A 2026 survey testing these exact fee levels found that 69% of respondents would not have enrolled in a U.S. program under the $70,000 initial fee plus $30,000 STEM-extension fee. While not nationally representative, it confirms the foreseeable deterrent effect.

DHS's own analysis acknowledges potential losses in work experience and earnings, employer productivity, school enrollment and revenue, and wider economic contributions, yet cannot quantify them and uses unpaid fees as a proxy. A fee is not a valid measure of the social value of research, innovation, teaching, entrepreneurship, or knowledge spillovers. Nor can affected parties always “cost share”: benefits are dispersed across firms, institutions, communities, and future innovations, while payment is immediate and concentrated.

The proposal also discounts reliance interests. Current students chose U.S. programs, paid tuition, relocated, and planned multiyear degrees under a longstanding framework that included possible OPT upon meeting legal requirements. Imposing a five- or six-figure condition on students already deep into their programs is not meaningfully prospective because their recommendation occurs after the effective date. At minimum, any change should exempt students enrolled before a final rule, but withdrawal is the proper course.

Less harmful alternatives include DSO training; risk-based audits and employer site visits; stronger SEVIS analytics; verification of degree-related work; targeted action against sham schools and repeat violators; clearer wage and worker protections; and penalties for proven misconduct. GAO recommended risk assessment, better data, monitoring, and training; measures that are more precise than wealth-based exclusion.

I oppose the proposed $70,000 OPT fee and any attempt to eliminate OPT because both risk weakening the American economy, harming businesses and workers, undermining universities, and transferring skilled talent and economic growth to competing countries.

1. The Policy Could Harm the American Economy Rather Than Protect It

The argument that international graduates take jobs from Americans assumes that the number of jobs in the economy is fixed. This is economically incomplete.

Skilled employees help businesses increase productivity, develop products, conduct research, and expand, creating additional opportunities for American workers.

A 2019 study in Labour Economics found that increased foreign STEM labor supply was associated with a 4.67% increase in average wages for existing U.S.-born STEM workers, largely through productivity and innovation spillovers.

Reducing international employment does not automatically create jobs or increase American wages. DHS has not demonstrated that this fee will benefit American workers.

2. Eliminating OPT Would Make These Problems Worse, Not Solve Them

Eliminating OPT would remove an established pathway for American-educated graduates to contribute to U.S. businesses.

Employers could lose access to qualified graduates, making it harder to fill specialized positions, conduct research, develop technologies, and expand operations.

Eliminating OPT does not guarantee those positions will go to Americans. Employers might reduce operations, relocate overseas, or outsource work to countries with lower labor costs.

Meanwhile, international graduates may take their skills to competing economies, transferring economic benefits away from the United States.

3. The United States Risks Exporting Its Own Educational Investment

International students pay tuition to American universities, spend money in local communities, and contribute to research and economic activity. After investing years and substantial resources in American education, many seek to apply their skills to American businesses through OPT.

If financial barriers prevent them from working here, they may take their expertise elsewhere, transferring skilled labor, innovation, and future economic growth to competing countries.

Why should the United States educate international talent only to create barriers that encourage graduates to contribute their skills and productivity elsewhere?

Lower-income graduates could be particularly disadvantaged if universities pass the costs to students or employers, making employment opportunities depend increasingly on family wealth rather than ability.

4. Individual Job Competition Stories Do Not Establish That OPT Harms American Workers Overall

American graduates' frustration with unemployment deserves to be taken seriously. However, individual hiring experiences cannot establish OPT's overall economic impact.

Employers generally seek qualified American candidates. When they cannot find available Americans who meet their requirements, hiring qualified international graduates allows businesses to fill positions and continue operating.

Claiming that an international student stole an American's job requires evidence that a qualified and available American worker was actually passed over. Without evidence of discrimination or unlawful hiring, an individual hiring decision does not establish that OPT harms American workers.

Blaming international graduates without establishing the actual cause of unemployment does not solve the problem. The question is whether restricting OPT creates more opportunities for Americans or simply makes American businesses less competitive.

5. Neither Charging an Extraordinary Fee Nor Eliminating OPT Is an Appropriate Way to Prevent Fraud

Even if DHS has concerns about OPT fraud, a $70,000 fee is not an effective or targeted solution. It does not distinguish legitimate students from those involved in fraudulent employment. Compliant students face the same financial barrier.

Paying $70,000 does not make employment legitimate, and being unable to afford it does not indicate fraud.

Eliminating OPT is no better. It does not identify fraudulent employers, distinguish legitimate employment from sham arrangements, or improve fraud detection. It simply eliminates the pathway for everyone, including students, universities, and employers that fully comply with the law.

The existence of fraud does not justify abolishing an entire program. DHS should investigate employers, verify employment arrangements, conduct audits, and penalize proven violations.

Preventing fraud should mean targeting misconduct, not financially punishing legitimate participants or eliminating an entire employment pathway.

I support the proposed rule and urge DHS to finalize it. I also support the alternative in Section V.A, which would reapply the initial fee at each new degree level.

1. The program has outgrown what Congress designed (Sec. IV.B).
Congress capped H-1B visas at 85,000 a year. OPT has no cap. In 2016, DHS projected that STEM OPT would reach about 92,000 participants by 2026. By 2024 it already exceeded 165,000, alongside 194,554 participants in regular OPT. A regulatory training benefit now produces more work authorizations than the statutory work visa Congress actually created. An uncapped side door that dwarfs the front door is not "practical training." It is a parallel guest worker program that no statute authorizes. A fee set in line with H-1B costs restores parity and removes the incentive to route around the cap.

2. Fraud is documented, large, and growing faster than enforcement (Sec. IV.A).
DHS identified more than 10,000 OPT students tied to highly suspect employers, including phantom worksites and residential addresses with no employees present. One convicted defendant supplied false employment documents to 2,693 students. About 60 SEVP field representatives cover 6,186 certified schools. In 2020, the CIS Ombudsman warned that compliance resources were not scaled to the size of the program. Site visits only catch problems after the fact. A fee prevents them, because it changes incentives before a fraudulent authorization is ever issued.

3. Charging schools puts accountability where the gatekeeping happens (Sec. IV.C).
Designated school officials recommend OPT, often with no job offer in hand for the initial 12 months, and they currently pay no price for bad recommendations. Requiring payment before a SEVIS recommendation gives each institution a direct financial stake in every placement. Programs that function as visa mills will be priced out. Schools confident in their students will pay, or will partner with employers who value those students.

4. The rule levels the field for American graduates (Sec. IV.B).
OPT workers are generally exempt from FICA taxes for up to five years. That saves employers 7.65 percent of wages and gives them a built-in reason to prefer foreign hires over U.S. graduates. Recent computer science and computer engineering graduates face unemployment rates of 6.1 and 7.5 percent. The fee offsets a tax-driven cost advantage that U.S. workers cannot match.

5. Reliance interests are properly protected (Sec. VI).
The rule applies only going forward. It exempts anyone who receives a DSO recommendation before the effective date, delays the effective date by 60 days, and refunds the fee if no employment authorization is issued. By statute, the F-1 classification is for people coming "solely" to study. Only about 20 percent of F-1 students used OPT in 2024, so the core educational benefit of the visa is untouched.

6. Recommendations to strengthen the final rule:
a. Adopt the Section V.A alternative, so the $70,000 initial fee applies at each new degree level. This closes the "degree-hopping" pattern used to extend work authorization.
b. Expressly bar schools from recovering the fee through tuition charged to U.S. students. The cost should fall on the participants and employers who benefit.
c. Publish annual data on fee collections, refunds, OPT participation by school, and employer compliance findings, so the public can judge whether the rule is working.
d. Strengthen the record on legal authority under INA 214(a) and HSA 102. Document how the fee amount relates to the deterrence goal and to existing H-1B costs, so the rule holds up on judicial review.
e. Pair the fee with mandatory E-Verify and I-983-style training plans for all post-completion OPT, as DHS indicated it may do in later phases.

This rule is a measured first step. It does not abolish OPT. It requires that participation be worth paying for. I urge DHS to finalize it promptly.

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) proposing exorbitant fees of $70,000 for initial OPT and $30,000 for subsequent OPT for F-1 nonimmigrant students. While I recognize the Department’s stated goals of protecting system integrity and combating fraud, these proposed fees are deeply punitive, economically counterproductive, and fundamentally arbitrary. If enacted, this rule will devastate higher education institutions, cripple the U.S. economy's ability to attract top global talent, and effectively abolish the legal pathway for practical training.

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule for the following critical reasons:

1. Prohibitive Financial Barriers and Economic Disproportion
The proposed fees of $70,000 for initial OPT and $30,000 for subsequent extensions are entirely unmoored from any reasonable administrative cost-recovery model. Most international students invest significant personal and family savings to pursue higher education in the United States. Requiring an upfront or post-graduation payment tens of thousands of dollars higher than the tuition of many degree programs makes OPT financially impossible for the vast majority of qualified students. This transforms a temporary, merit-based work authorization program into an exclusionary luxury available only to the ultra-wealthy.

2. Severe Damage to U.S. Higher Education Competitiveness
U.S. universities rely on international students to enrich academic environments, support research, and contribute billions of dollars to local and national economies. Optional Practical Training, particularly the STEM extension, is a vital, legally established component of the F-1 educational experience, providing students with critical real-world application of their studies. Imposing these crippling fees will cause international student enrollment to plummet as prospective students choose more welcoming destination countries like Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, and Germany, where post-study work pathways remain accessible and reasonably priced.

3. Undermining Key U.S. Industries and Workforce Needs
U.S. employers across technology, engineering, healthcare, finance, and advanced manufacturing face chronic talent shortages. OPT serves as a vital bridge allowing graduates to transition into the U.S. workforce, often serving as the primary pipeline for H-1B filings and high-skilled employment. By erecting a $70,000 financial wall, DHS will deny employers access to the world-class graduates trained by American universities. Rather than "protecting U.S. workers," starving vital sectors of specialized talent harms innovation, decreases domestic productivity, and incentivizes companies to offshore research, development, and high-tech jobs.

4. Disproportionate Burden on Entry-Level Workers
OPT is designed for recent graduates who are, by definition, at the very beginning of their professional careers. Entry-level salaries for practical training participants rarely accommodate an immediate out-of-pocket burden of $70,000, nor can standard entry-level employers reasonably absorb such a fee on behalf of temporary interns or junior staff. This fee acts as an absolute market exclusion rather than a regulatory safeguard.

5. Lack of Narrowly Tailored Solutions to Combat Fraud
While DHS cites fraud prevention as a primary justification, imposing a catastrophic, across-the-board financial barrier is an overbroad and disproportionate policy mechanism. Existing enforcement mechanisms, such as enhanced employer validation, SEVIS tracking, and strict reporting requirements through Designated School Officials (DSOs), already exist to police bad actors. Penalizing thousands of legitimate, law-abiding students and hurting American academic institutions to target isolated instances of fraud is neither sound public policy nor an effective regulatory solution.

Conclusion
The proposed OPT fee rule threatens to inflict long-term damage on the global preeminence of the U.S. higher education system and weaken the competitiveness of the American economy. I respectfully request that DHS withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety.

3. Is this really a fee, or a way to price students out of OPT?

I am a graduate student worker studying neurodegeneration in the Department of Neuroscience at Yale University. I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule under Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, which would charge $70,000 for an F-1 student’s first Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendation and $30,000 for each one after that.

Neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s are diseases of aging, and they are difficult to model. No single model fully reproduces human disease, so researchers often combine several models and approaches to build a reliable picture. Mouse models are central to this work, but the pathology we study develops slowly. Mice must be bred, often across multiple genetic crosses, and then aged for many months before the disease features we want to study appear. Only then can behavioral testing, tissue analysis, and molecular experiments begin, and those need to be repeated and validated. A single well-controlled study can take well over a year from the first breeding to usable data. Because the experiments themselves are slow, training in this field takes longer. A PhD student, like me, studying neurodegeneration often reaches the point of collecting key data late in their program, and the work that follows (replication, analysis, writing, and publication) frequently extends beyond graduation. OPT is what allows an international trainee to stay and complete that work as a postdoctoral researcher. Without it, projects that took years to set up would be left unfinished, aged animal cohorts would be wasted, and the training invested in the scientist who ran them would be lost. 

A fee of this size would break the link between training and employment. Few employers, whether a university lab or a small biotech startup, can justify a five-figure surcharge to hire a single early-career scientist, and no trainee can pay it out of pocket. Having worked in both academic and industry settings, I have seen how a discovery travels from the bench to the clinic. Findings typically begin in university labs and are then developed by biotech and pharmaceutical teams. The people who carry that work across are often early-career scientists who trained in one setting and were hired into the other. OPT is a major part of that handoff for international researchers. If these researchers never begin U.S. training or leave once they finish, the expertise and the public investment in their education leave with them.

Neurodegenerative diseases affect millions of American families, and the work to treat them is slow and cumulative. Narrowing the pool of people allowed to do that work will slow it further. It would also weaken the biotechnology sector and the jobs it creates, and it would encourage the strongest applicants to choose other countries that actively recruit international scientists, eroding U.S. leadership in biomedical research.

For these reasons, I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule.

5. The OPT fee could deter legitimate training more effectively than fraud
Public comment on Optional Practical Training Fees
DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100
91 Fed. Reg. 64,566 (Oct. 8, 2026)
I ask DHS to withdraw the proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees rule. DHS predicts that a large fee will discourage abuse and give schools a greater stake in screening recommendations. That prediction depends on who bears the fee and how legitimate and fraudulent participants respond. The proposal does not adequately test either link.
DHS should evaluate who leaves and who stays
A school or employer offering a genuine placement weighs the fee against the value of supervised training. That value can be substantial even when the placement brings in little revenue. An organized scheme could have different incentives. A broker might raise the price it charges students, pool financing, or concentrate its business in placements where it can recover the cost. The fee could make some schemes uneconomic. The record needs to explain which schemes would exit, which could adapt, and how those responses compare with the expected exit of legitimate programs.
For example, assume a program starts with 1,000 legitimate placements and 20 fraudulent ones. If a fee deters 500 legitimate placements and five fraudulent ones, the number of fraudulent placements falls, but their share rises from about 2 percent to about 3 percent. This illustration is not a forecast. It shows why total participation, fraud prevalence, and the number of violations prevented are different measures. DHS should assess all three and explain how their movement would affect investigative workload and the likelihood of identifying violations.
Pass-through also changes the screening incentive
The preamble predicts schools will screen more carefully because they bear a financial stake. The economic analysis also anticipates that schools may shift the charge to students or employers. A school that collects the full amount before it recommends a student still faces administrative and compliance risks, but it does not bear the same financial exposure as a school paying from its own budget. DHS should separately analyze school-funded, employer-funded, and student-funded recommendations and explain how each arrangement affects screening. It should compare the fee with controls directed at facts a broker cannot establish merely by producing payment, such as whether a worksite exists and whether it provides the training it claims to offer.
Under 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A), finalizing the proposal would be arbitrary and capricious if DHS continues to assume that a smaller pool is a better-screened pool without examining these countervailing incentives. DHS should withdraw the proposed rule.

I am writing to express my strong support for the proposed rule establishing fees for F-1 students engaging in Optional Practical Training ($70,000 for initial OPT; $30,000 for subsequent OPT). The OPT program has grown far beyond its original educational scope, often serving as an uncapped labor pathway without sufficient oversight. This proposed fee structure is a necessary measure to:
- Combat Fraud: Deterring bad actors and institutions from misusing student status primarily for commercial employment.
- Address High Recent-Grad Unemployment & Tax Inequalities: Recent U.S. college graduates face elevated unemployment and underemployment. Allowing uncapped foreign labor directly harms domestic degree-holders struggling to launch early careers. Compounding this issue, F-1 students on OPT are exempt from FICA taxes (Social Security and Medicare), saving employers 7.65% in payroll taxes per hire. This tax loophole gives foreign graduates an unfair financial advantage over U.S. citizens.   
- Restore Integrity: Ensuring higher education institutions maintain strict accountability when recommending post-graduate work authorization.
I urge the Department to finalize and enforce these fee requirements as proposed.

STOP OPT AND LET AMERICAN TAKE THE JOBS
Optional Practical Training (OPT) was created out of thin air and needs to be eliminated. However, until the program is terminated, I support the proposed fees. DHS is right that the F-1 visa “was never intended to provide a pathway to employment in the United States.” A student visa is for study, and it should end with the degree. OPT provides a multi-year work permit that Congress never approved. There is no statutory authorization for foreign students to engage in work in the United States. There are no wage requirements or numerical limits. And, there are no protections for American workers who must compete with foreign students seeking to work in the United States. The proposed fee will deter use of the OPT program and prioritize deserving American students.
